title: Cakes No. 1
altText: A pastel drawing of cakes in the colorful, sweet-treat style of the American artist Wayne Thiebaud, drawn on cream-colored tracing paper. Details of the arrangement and exact colors have not been confirmed from the museum record.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (American, 1920-2021), date, medium, dimensions (44.5 x 47.4 cm), credit line and public-domain flag (false) read from the record. The record has no description, so the text stays close to the title and medium. No image linked because the work is in copyright.

context: A pastel drawing made in 1967 by the American artist Wayne Thiebaud, who is widely known for paintings and drawings of cakes, pies and other everyday foods. The Art Institute's record lists the medium as pastel on cream tracing paper and gives no further description.

descriptions.k: Yum, this picture is about cakes! Wayne Thiebaud drew it with soft, colorful chalk called pastel. Look for the cake and the frosting. What colors do you see? What flavor would you pick?
descriptions.g12: Wayne Thiebaud drew cakes with pastels, which are soft sticks of color like chalk. He did it on cream-colored paper that you can almost see through. He liked to make everyday sweets look special. What colors do you see on the cakes? Do they make you want to taste them?
descriptions.g35: Wayne Thiebaud was an American artist famous for pictures of cakes, pies, and other everyday foods. In Cakes No. 1, he used pastel on cream tracing paper, which is thin and smooth. Pastel gives rich color with a soft, chalky surface. Why might an artist choose a bakery treat as a subject, and how does the soft pastel change the way a cake looks?
descriptions.g68: Wayne Thiebaud made art about ordinary foods such as cakes, which connected him to Pop art even though his work was often painterly and warm. In this 1967 pastel on tracing paper, color is built from soft, chalky strokes. The museum record gives only the date and medium, so close looking matters. How does choosing a humble, shared subject like cake shape the way viewers feel about it, and what does pastel add compared with paint?
descriptions.g910: In Cakes No. 1, Thiebaud treats a commonplace dessert as a subject worthy of careful drawing. Pastel on tracing paper emphasizes vivid, powdery color and a delicate surface, qualities that suit the sweetness of the subject. His work is often linked to Pop art because of its everyday subject matter, though its handmade touch sets it apart from mass-produced imagery. Consider what is gained and lost when a mass-market treat is rendered with careful, tender attention.
descriptions.g1112: Thiebaud's cakes occupy an ambiguous position between Pop art's engagement with consumer goods and a more traditional still-life interest in light, color, and form. In this 1967 pastel on translucent tracing paper, the delicacy of the medium contrasts with the abundance of the subject. The Art Institute's record provides only essential data, so claims about symbolism require caution. Viewers might read the work as celebration, nostalgia, or quiet commentary on abundance; the visual evidence of color and handling must carry the argument.

k.daily: What flavor of cake would you pick from this picture? Tell us what you see that helps you choose.
k.emotion: Does this picture make you feel happy, hungry, or calm? Tell us why.
k.observation: Look for the cake and the frosting. What colors can you find?
k.analysis: Where does your eye go first in the picture? What makes it stop there?
k.line: Trace the edge of a cake in the air. Does it go straight, or does it curve?
k.shape: Cakes have shapes like circles, triangles, or blocks. Which shapes do you spot?
k.color: Which color looks the yummiest to you? Where does it appear?
k.texture: Pastel is soft and chalky. How does the picture look soft, like frosting?
k.space: Does the cake look close to you or far away? How can you tell?
k.light: Do any parts of the cake look like they have a bright spot? Point to them.
k.meaning: Why would an artist want to draw cakes?
k.culture: Cakes are shared at birthdays and parties. When do you eat cake with others?
k.technique: Pastel sticks are like chalk. What do you think happens when you smudge them with your finger?
k.personal: Tell about the best cake you have ever seen or tasted.
k.critical: Real cakes get eaten, but a drawing stays. How is a cake in a drawing different from one on a plate?

g12.daily: What are the first colors you notice, and how do they make the cakes look?
g12.emotion: What feeling does this picture give you, sweet, cozy, or playful? What makes you feel that way?
g12.observation: List what you see on the paper. How many cakes or pieces of cake can you find?
g12.analysis: How does the artist arrange the cakes so the picture feels organized?
g12.line: Look for edges where one color meets another. How do those edges help you see the cakes?
g12.shape: Describe the shapes of the cakes. How do the shapes repeat or change?
g12.color: Find the colors that look the sweetest and the ones that look the plainest. How do they work together?
g12.texture: Pastel makes powdery color. Where does the surface look soft and creamy?
g12.space: The paper is thin and cream-colored. How does it show through the pastel?
g12.light: Where does the artist make the frosting look bright? Where does it look shaded?
g12.meaning: Thiebaud liked to draw everyday foods. What does that tell you about what he noticed?
g12.culture: Cakes are treats for celebrations in many places. What celebrations do you know that have cake?
g12.technique: Pastel is rubbed and layered on paper. How might that help make soft, bright color?
g12.personal: If you drew your favorite dessert, what colors would you pick?
g12.critical: Why might drawing a simple treat be a good way to practice looking carefully?

g35.daily: What do you notice first in this drawing, and what choices by Thiebaud lead your eye there?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the mood of this drawing? Which colors or shapes create it?
g35.observation: Spend a minute looking carefully. Which small details of color and edge did you notice late?
g35.analysis: How does Thiebaud organize the cakes and the space around them on the page?
g35.line: How do edges between colors replace outlines in a pastel drawing?
g35.shape: How do the cake shapes repeat or differ, and how does that create rhythm?
g35.color: Pastel gives strong, powdery color. How do the colors on the cakes work together?
g35.texture: How would you describe the surface of pastel on tracing paper, and how does it suit a creamy subject?
g35.space: How does the cream-colored paper help create the space around the cakes?
g35.light: How does the artist suggest light and shadow on the frosting using only color?
g35.meaning: Why might a cake be a good subject for an artist who wants us to notice everyday life?
g35.culture: Thiebaud's cakes are linked to American bakeries and cafeterias. What does food say about a culture?
g35.technique: How is working in pastel on thin paper different from painting in oil on canvas?
g35.personal: What everyday thing could you study as carefully as Thiebaud studied cakes?
g35.critical: The museum record has few details. How can careful looking add to what the record tells you?

g68.daily: How does Thiebaud make a simple cake seem worth studying as much as a famous landscape or portrait?
g68.emotion: How do the sweet subject and the soft, chalky color combine to create a feeling?
g68.observation: Describe the arrangement of the cakes and the empty paper around them. What do you notice about the balance?
g68.analysis: How does the composition guide your eye across the drawing?
g68.line: How do color edges take the place of drawn outlines to define the cakes?
g68.shape: How do the geometry of the cakes and the repetition of forms create a sense of order?
g68.color: How do contrasts of bright and pale pastel color make the cakes look tempting?
g68.texture: How does the powdery quality of pastel suggest the softness of frosting and cake?
g68.space: How does the pale ground function as an open space around the cakes?
g68.light: How does Thiebaud use color shifts to create light and shadow without detailed shading?
g68.meaning: Why might an artist choose an everyday dessert as a serious subject, and how does that fit with Pop art's interest in common things?
g68.culture: What does a picture of cakes tell you about celebrations, food, and American life in the 1960s?
g68.technique: What are the advantages and challenges of pastel compared with paint when making rich color?
g68.personal: When does an ordinary object become meaningful to you? How could you draw it?
g68.critical: Does a humble subject make a work less important or more? Support your view with something from the drawing.

g910.daily: How does the drawing balance tenderness toward its subject with a cool, repetitive look?
g910.emotion: How does color alone make the cakes appealing, and what other feelings might be mixed in?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy of cakes, color accents, and the paper. What draws your attention first?
g910.analysis: Analyze how the arrangement of cakes and empty space establishes a calm, ordered composition.
g910.line: How do edges formed by color change replace conventional outlines, and what does that do for the forms?
g910.shape: How do simple geometric forms contribute to the sense of a staged still life?
g910.color: How does the saturation and softness of pastel shape the drawing's sweetness?
g910.texture: How does pastel's powdery surface differ from painted surfaces, and how does it affect the experience of the subject?
g910.space: How does the pale, translucent ground set off the cakes and affect depth?
g910.light: How might Thiebaud use color shifts around forms to suggest glowing light and shadow?
g910.meaning: In what ways could a drawing of cakes comment on abundance, ritual, or consumer culture, and what limits our confidence in those readings?
g910.culture: How does the choice of cake connect Thiebaud to Pop art, and how does his approach differ from mass-produced imagery?
g910.technique: Why might pastel on tracing paper be a suitable choice for an artist interested in color and delicate surfaces?
g910.personal: How do your own memories of sweets and celebrations shape the way you read this drawing?
g910.critical: How should viewers handle the gap between a limited museum record and a work that invites symbolic interpretation?

g1112.daily: What do you see in Cakes No. 1 that supports reading it as celebration, and what might complicate that reading?
g1112.emotion: How does the delicate medium complicate or deepen the feeling of abundance suggested by the subject?
g1112.observation: Describe the formal organization with precision. At what point does description of cakes start to imply a meaning?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how Thiebaud's composition arranges repeated forms against the open ground to create both order and charm.
g1112.line: How does the replacement of contour with color edge connect to the painterly tradition in which Thiebaud worked?
g1112.shape: How do the geometry of the cakes and their arrangement in space evoke both still-life convention and displays of goods?
g1112.color: How does pastel color, powdery and saturated, mediate between the appeal of sweets and the discipline of observation?
g1112.texture: How does the tactile quality of pastel on translucent paper complicate the cool impersonality sometimes associated with Pop art?
g1112.space: What is the effect of the pale, open ground on the cakes' presence and on the sense of display?
g1112.light: How does the suggestion of light through color rather than tone align the drawing with a modern approach to form?
g1112.meaning: Weigh competing readings: nostalgia, celebration of consumer abundance, or detached observation. What does the evidence permit?
g1112.culture: How does a subject associated with American bakeries and diners position the drawing in discussions of postwar consumer culture, and where do those discussions oversimplify?
g1112.technique: How does Thiebaud's use of a fragile medium and thin support shape the work's relationship to permanence and display?
g1112.personal: How do your own experiences of food and ritual influence your reading of an everyday still life?
g1112.critical: What standards should govern interpretations of a work with few documented intentions?

teacherNote.context: Wayne Thiebaud is best known for paintings and drawings of cakes, pies and other foods. The museum record for this 1967 pastel is brief, so the entry is cautious and should be revised once a person has seen the image. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students make a pastel or chalk drawing of a simple food, using colored edges instead of outlines.
Ask students to compare a drawing of a treat with a photo of the same treat and list what each shows best.
Discuss why artists choose everyday subjects and what students would choose from their own lives.
